[1] [Mad studies and social work: Conceptualising the subjectivities of service user/survivors who experience significant mental health problems](https://consensus.app/papers/details/w:b8fea9fe-3113-456b-b55a-946c4ddb6f03/?utm_source=claude_desktop) (Stephen J. Macdonald et al., 2018, 5 citations, Social Work and Social Sciences Review)
  id: w:b8fea9fe-3113-456b-b55a-946c4ddb6f03
  This article draws on contemporary and classical psycho–political theorists to conceptualise ‘mental illness’ as a social construct. The research employs a Mad Studies and anti-psychiatry perspective to reframe ‘mental illness’ from an individualised pathological defect to a socially constructed reality (Foucault, 1967; Menzies et al., 2013). The study applies a qualitative biographical methodology to analyse the subjectivities of people with severe mental health problems, their family members and mental health practitioners. In this study, once individuals were conceptualised as pathologically ‘ill’ they were then medicated and often institutionalised as a form of ‘treatment’. The findings present a theoretical analysis of participants’ subjectivities to examine historic and contemporary psychiatric practices. The article will conclude by discussing how Mad Studies can offer social work practice an alternative theoretical standpoint to conceptualise ‘mental illness’ as a social rather than a pathological phenomenon.Keywords: mad studies; anti-psychiatry movement; ‘mental illness’; biographical methodology; institutionalisation; medicalisation; family

[2] [From Mental Illness to Disability](https://consensus.app/papers/details/w:23290611-b826-448b-9670-1836284625c3/?utm_source=claude_desktop) (Bhargavi V. Davar, 2008, 21 citations, Indian Journal of Gender Studies)
  id: w:23290611-b826-448b-9670-1836284625c3
  This article traces the critical engagement of the women's movement with psychiatry, mental health and disability in India over the past two decades. Three phases can be discerned in this history. The first was a phase of radical intellectual disbelief about the very existence of mental illness as a valid knowledge category. In the second phase the experiential reality of women, who had to engage with their own emotional states, found expression in a variety of discourses about women and mental health. The marginalisation of women by the mainstream medical sciences was addressed, and the right to care was redefined as the creation of gender-sensitive sciences. In the third and present phase I interrogate the paths we have taken in the creation of such gender-sensitive mental health practices. A mental illness language has been exhausted of any positive content. The rights orientation to mental health can be developed from disability thinking, which is providing an alternative vision for the world, as well for persons labelled mentally ill.

[3] [From Mental Illness to Disability: Choices for Women Users/Survivors of Psychiatry in Self and Identity Constructions](https://consensus.app/papers/details/w:5d78e345-ad35-4b62-a0ad-c73b664c6fd6/?utm_source=claude_desktop) (Bhargavi V. Davar, 2020, 11 citations, Routledge eBooks)
  id: w:5d78e345-ad35-4b62-a0ad-c73b664c6fd6
  This chapter aims to describe the engagement of the women's movement with mental illness through the 1990s, articulating the contested areas vis-a-vis feminist politics and psychiatry. The gains of using a language of disability over a language of mental illness in order to remain close to personal experience of psychological suffering are explored in this paper. Das and Addlakha's paper, one of the few available providing case studies of psychiatric disability, assumes that the two, that is, mental illness and psychosocial disability, are co-terminus. This paper is an attempt in this direction, using a historicising approach that examines what all these concepts have meant for women users/survivors of psychiatry. Healing discourses that are aimed to nurture the spirit are built on a philosophy of unconditional love , whereas political activism is built on finding suitable channels for women's rage. Safe spaces were created for personal disclosures, as women with similar experiences found each other and shared their stories.

[4] [From “Care and Custody” to the “Project of Life”: A Semiotic Study of Legal Discourse on Disability and Mental Illness in Italy (20th–21st Centuries)](https://consensus.app/papers/details/w:584ed5e9-947a-4d7f-9a8d-8500b35c4ec7/?utm_source=claude_desktop) (Jenny Ponzo, 2025, 3 citations, International Journal for the Semiotics of Law - Revue internationale de Sémiotique juridique)
  id: w:584ed5e9-947a-4d7f-9a8d-8500b35c4ec7
  In Western culture, people with mental illness and disabilities have long been labeled as deviant and abnormal. This notion was linked to the development of institutions aimed at removing these people from the view of “normal” members of society and denying interaction with them. Confinement in special institutions, such as psychiatric hospitals, was described as necessary to protect both the “sick” or “abnormal” person and society, and this ideology survived into the twentieth century. From the second half of the century, however, a new sensibility began to emerge and take root, and a path towards full recognition of the rights, dignity and freedom of people with disabilities and mental illness began. Italy was the first European country to abolish psychiatric hospitals and special classes for disabled students. This article therefore proposes a semiotic analysis of the evolution of legal discourse in Italy, starting from a 1904 law on the management of the “insane”, then focusing on the laws of 1968 and 1978. Attention is also given to the 2006 United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, adopted by Italy in 2009, and the subsequent Italian law of 2021, which fully recognizes the subjectivity of people with disabilities and grants them the right to shape their lives according to their needs and desires, in a fully visible – namely socially integrated – way, with a mentality that reverses the old one that marginalized these categories of people by confining and hiding them in dehumanizing institutions.

[5] [Madness as disability](https://consensus.app/papers/details/w:54384a7c-c8f7-4285-a4cd-de7ae88bb2f8/?utm_source=claude_desktop) (Sander L. Gilman, 2014, 17 citations, History of Psychiatry)
  id: w:54384a7c-c8f7-4285-a4cd-de7ae88bb2f8
  How does society imagine mental illness? Does this shift radically over time and with different social attitudes as well as scientific discoveries about the origins and meanings of mental illness? What happens when we begin to think about mental illness as madness, as a malleable concept constantly shifting its meaning? We thus look at the meanings associated with 'general paralysis of the insane' in the nineteenth century and autism today in regard to disability. In this case study we examine the claims by scholars such as the anthropologist Emily Martin and the psychiatrist Kay Jamison as to the relationship between mental illness, disability and creativity. Today, the health sciences have become concerned with mental illness as a form of disability. How does this change the meaning of madness for practitioners and patients?

© The Author(s) 2014.

[6] [Disability Studies and the Language of Mental Illness](https://consensus.app/papers/details/w:4d2a4947-5d78-470d-b777-20bd92e8b8d8/?utm_source=claude_desktop) (Katie Aubrecht, 2012, 27 citations, The review of disability studies/Review of disability studies)
  id: w:4d2a4947-5d78-470d-b777-20bd92e8b8d8
  Much has been written about the dangers of mental illness, both by psychiatry as an empirical reality and by anti-psychiatry as a cultural category (Szasz, 1960). This paper considers how the language of mental illness, and more specifically, the discipline of psychiatry, structures how we relate to our everyday lives. I examine how the language of mental illness, and the psychiatric practices which have made this language possible, have conditioned the development of a disability studies community, culture and identity. This examination will involve a critical analysis of writing in the field of disability studies which illustrates the complex interconnections and interdependencies between self-identifying as a disabled person and rediscovering the aspects of oneself that have been stolen or stamped out by the imposition of a language of mental illness. This paper also aims to uncover some of the implicit assumptions about the nature of the relationship between language, culture, identity, and community.

# Population umbrellas: does "mobility" make sense as an identity, and what should the identity lens hold?

**Status:** advisory memo for the owner. Population taxonomy is the owner's doctrine: this memo RECOMMENDS and decides nothing. It changes no file, row, ruling or task.
**Written:** 2026-11-12, by a Fable-class researcher-analyst, in answer to the owner's two questions of that day and under the owner's statements "thirteenth" (MOB decomposes) and "fourteenth" ("use advocacy groups and disability ethics as a lens for grouping/sorting/taxonomy").
**Drift warning:** every statement about the database was read from `data/guidebook.db` on 2026-11-12 (read-only). No count is quoted as a fact to trust; each carries the command that regenerates it (section 9). Every web source was retrieved on 2026-11-12; nothing was written to the retrieval log or the database, so nothing here is an admitted source.

**Claim marks.** VERIFIED = I retrieved the page or record and read the passage. INFERRED = my reasoning, basis stated. UNVERIFIED = I believe it but did not retrieve it; do not rely on it.

**The unratified assumption this memo works under** (ledger, fourteenth statement): "advocacy groups" means disabled people's own organisations, the CRPD's "representative organizations", not charities or service bodies speaking for them. The CRPD Committee draws that line itself (General Comment No. 7, paras 11 and 13, section 2.1). Every organisation below is flagged where the retrieved page did not show it to be led by disabled people.

---

## 0. Verdict

**Q1. Does "mobility" make sense as an identity population? No.** In the sources retrieved, disabled people do not organise as "people with mobility needs". They organise across disability (Council of Canadians with Disabilities, ENIL), by condition or impairment (spinal cord injury, spina bifida and hydrocephalus, limb loss and limb difference), and by device ("all wheelchair users", United Spinal Association). "Mobility" is the name of a functional domain (ICF chapter d4, the Washington Group's walking question, CRPD Article 20 on personal mobility as a right). `MOB` conflates four different kinds of fact: a function, a set of impairments, the use of an assistive device, and a number of separate communities. The owner's decomposition is correct, but its branches are not all identities: aid type and power-versus-manual are **device** facts; paraplegia-versus-quadriplegia is an **impairment-level** fact; only some branches (limb loss and limb difference, spinal cord injury, wheelchair users) correspond to communities that organise under that name. The design parameters the project has actually researched depend on the device and its user's function, not on a community.

**Q2. Do contemporary advocates think like this? Not in this form.** They hold several layers at once: a cross-disability political identity ("disabled people", "nothing about us without us"); specific communities named on their own terms, some of which reject the impairment frame altogether (Deaf people as a linguistic and cultural group; users and survivors of psychiatry rather than "people with mental health conditions"); device-defined constituencies whose edges are contested (ambulatory wheelchair users); and, separately, functional categories that statisticians use and that advocates treat as tools, not identities. Broad impairment umbrellas ("mobility", "neurological", "mental health") are the administrative layer, not the self-defined one.

**Q3. What do modern ethical approaches propose?** They converge on three points and disagree on a fourth. (1) Classify the **environment's demand and the barrier**, not the person (social model, CRPD, ICF environmental factors, universal design). (2) Where people are named, **they name themselves**, through their own organisations (CRPD Art. 4.3 and General Comment No. 7, epistemic justice, disability justice's "leadership of those most impacted"). (3) Keep the **individual** in view: categories are retrieval aids, never portraits (capabilities approach, care ethics, crip critique, the project's own irreducibility principle). They disagree on (4) whether impairment-specific categories should exist at all: disability justice and the social model press toward cross-disability solidarity and warn about hierarchies of impairment; community self-definition and the capabilities approach press toward specificity. The reconciliation the evidence supports is to keep the two jobs apart: communities for **voice and provenance**, access needs / ICF / device for **design parameters**.

**RECOMMENDATION (the owner decides).** Keep the four lens columns exactly as ruled on 2026-08-28. Change what the **identity** lens is allowed to contain: only communities that disabled people have organised and named themselves, each row carrying the organisation or ethical source it rests on as provenance (the fourteenth statement's own ACTION 2). Retire `MOB` as an identity; hold "mobility" where it already lives, as ICF d4 codes and access needs. Hold device in `device_class` and nowhere else. Hold family resemblance (the "mobility family", the "neurodivergent" coalition) as a parent relation in data, used for navigation and for finding commonality, never as the key of a determination unless the family passes the ratified design-equivalence test. Record who co-produced a source as a typed relation to a community, separately from whom a determination serves. This is option 2 with option 3's hierarchy held as data, and option 4's separation of provenance from the key (section 7).

**Confidence.** High (about 85%) that `MOB` is not an identity and that device and impairment level are not identities. Moderate (about 70%) that restricting the identity lens to self-organised communities is the right rule. Low to moderate (about 50%) on the particular list of communities, because my sample of organisations is international-umbrella and Anglophone (Canada, United States, United Kingdom, Europe), no non-English national organisation was retrieved, and several key organisations could not be reached (section 10).

**What would change it.** (a) Evidence that organisations *of* physically disabled people, as such, are a common form outside English (the United Kingdom's Union of the Physically Impaired Against Segregation, 1975, is one; I did not retrieve any current national federation of this kind, and I think it likely that several exist: UNVERIFIED). That would support a "physical disability" community row, though still not "mobility". (b) Co-1 evidence that a design parameter varies by community membership after device and function are held fixed. (c) The owner ruling that the identity lens is meant as a reader's entry point rather than as a statement about communities, in which case administrative umbrellas are tolerable as entry aliases, provided they key nothing.

---

## 1. What the project's own rulings and rows say (read first, so the rest is not relitigated)

All VERIFIED by reading `references/project-standards.md` (locate each with the grep in section 9) and the database.

1. **Work from axes, no armchair umbrellas** (2026-07-22). The profile layer "is populated only with specific self-identified communities named on their own terms (co-produced; 'nothing about us without us')". "Physically disabled / wheelchair users" is named there as one of three self-caught erasures.
2. **Design-equivalence exception** (2026-07-23). An umbrella is permitted only if (a) high comorbidity or near-identical design profile, (b) the union of member signatures is preserved, (c) no opposed demand between members. `COM` and `BRAIN` were ratified under it.
3. **`MOB` is split** into ambulatory (`AMB`) and wheelchair user (`WHEEL`), "to start" (2026-08-25, marked not to be relitigated). The entry itself says `MOB` fails clause (c) and that part-time wheelchair users and balance are covered by neither new code.
4. **"Population" is retired; four lenses** identity / icf / needs / medical; four typed lens columns with real foreign keys; CHECK relaxed to at least one (2026-08-28, D-0182).
5. **The medical lens grows on demand**, and the ledger already observed that the wheeled-mobility literature "studies wheelchairs, scooters and walking aids, not diagnoses" (2026-09-11).
6. **`ALL` is a scope marker, not a population** (2026-11-06, hedged by the owner).
7. **Thirteenth and fourteenth statements** (2026-11-12): `MOB` is a family with more than two levels; advocacy groups and disability ethics are the lens. The thirteenth entry's own ACTION 3 already says a division describing a device or a participant's level is kept in one home (rule 5) and that whether it is an identity or a descriptor is the owner's to decide.

**The registry does not match the rulings.** VERIFIED:

- `base_taxonomy_identity` still carries `MOB` as `active`, and carries no `AMB` or `WHEEL` row, although the split was ratified on 2026-08-25. `parent_code` is empty on every row.
- `MOB` carries the large majority of `source_value_extractions` rows; the other identity codes in use there are `ALL`, `SCI`, `BLIND` and `MS`, each with a handful.
- Almost every extraction states the identity lens only; the ICF and needs lenses are used on a handful of rows and the medical lens on none. The project's rule is to work from the ICF and access-need frame; the rows work from the umbrella.
- `device_class` is filled on a minority of the `MOB` rows; where it is filled the values in use are `manual_self_propelled`, `mixed` and `not_device_scoped`. The column's CHECK also allows `manual_attendant`, `power_chair`, `scooter`, `bariatric_manual`, `bariatric_power` and `walker_rollator`, none of which is in use. So the registry of devices exists, as a CHECK list, and already holds the first two of the owner's three decompositions (aid type; power versus manual).
- What the `MOB` rows actually name, from `root_population_note` where filled: manual self-propelled wheelchair users; "eleven wheelchair users; chair types not stated"; thirteen wheelchair users of whom at least one used a motorised chair; a first-person judgment by a manual wheelchair user about experienced self-propelling users; an aggregate of eight subject groups that "is not a wheelchair-only recommendation"; and organisations whose constituency is wider than wheelchair users (people with any disability or chronic illness) or different (people with intellectual disability). None names "people with mobility needs". The code is being used to mean "this is about getting about, mostly on wheels".
- Every `specifications` row is keyed on `MOB`, all are retired, and most state `design_scale = 'universal'`. A determination at universal scale keyed on an identity states two things that cannot both be meant: universal is the scale that names no group.
- `identity_icf_map` grades `MOB` to nine ICF d-codes (d410 to d530) as `high_predictive`. That is the highest confidence grade, given to a category the ledger says fails the umbrella test because its members' demands are opposed. Walking (d450), using equipment to move (d465), washing (d510) and toileting (d530) cannot all be predicted with high confidence from membership of a set that includes a prosthesis user, a power-chair user with tetraplegia and a person with a balance disorder. INFERRED from the map and the ledger entry.

---

## 2. The lens: how disabled people's own organisations define their constituencies

### 2.1 What counts as an organisation of disabled people

VERIFIED from the United Nations document CRPD/C/GC/7, *General comment No. 7 (2018) on the participation of persons with disabilities, including children with disabilities, through their representative organizations, in the implementation and monitoring of the Convention*, Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, distributed 9 November 2018 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3899396/files/CRPD_C_GC_7-EN.pdf):

- Para 11: organisations of persons with disabilities "can only be those that are led, directed and governed by persons with disabilities. A clear majority of their membership should be recruited among persons with disabilities themselves."
- Para 11(d): "They may represent one or more constituencies based on actual or perceived impairment or can be open to membership of all persons with disabilities". Para 11(e): they "can include constituencies based on transversal identities (for example, children, women or indigenous people with disabilities) and comprise members with various impairments".
- Para 12 names the types: umbrella organisations (which "only speak on behalf of their member organizations" and "cannot represent individual persons with disabilities"); cross-disability organisations; self-advocacy organisations, "especially persons with intellectual disabilities"; organisations including family members, for people with intellectual disabilities, dementia and children, whose role "should be to assist and empower"; organisations of women and girls; organisations of children and young persons. Para 12(a) adds: "persons with disabilities should be able to decide for themselves which organizations they want to represent them."
- Para 13: they "should be distinguished from organizations 'for' persons with disabilities, which provide services and/or advocate on behalf of persons with disabilities, which, in practice, may result in a conflict of interests".
- Para 50 gives the Committee's own list of who must be reached. It is not a taxonomy and mixes kinds freely: women, older persons, children, "those requiring high levels of support", victims of landmines, migrants, "persons with actual or perceived psychosocial impairments, persons with intellectual disabilities, neurodiverse persons, including those with autism or dementia, persons with albinism, permanent physical impairments, chronic pain, leprosy and visual impairments and persons who are deaf, deafblind or otherwise hearing-impaired".

Three things follow for a taxonomy. INFERRED from the paragraphs above. (i) The Committee accepts **three bases of constituency at once**: impairment ("actual or perceived"), open cross-disability membership, and transversal identity. It does not rank them. (ii) Constituency is **self-chosen**: the test is who leads and whom people choose to represent them, not which box a classifier puts them in. (iii) An umbrella speaks only for its members on agreed matters and cannot represent individuals. That is the Committee's version of this project's own anti-umbrella rule.

### 2.2 Advocacy-organisation table

Every row was built from the organisation's own page, retrieved 2026-11-12, except where marked. "Led by" is filled only from what the retrieved page states. Quotation marks enclose the page's words.

| # | Organisation | Scope / constituency as they define it | Membership basis | How they name themselves and their people | Reach | Led by disabled people? (from the retrieved page) | Source retrieved |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | International Disability Alliance (IDA) | "a global alliance of OPD networks"; "An alliance of 14 networks, made up of 5,500 organisations of persons with disabilities in 182 countries" | Umbrella of umbrellas: six regional cross-disability forums and eight global constituency organisations | "organisations of persons with disabilities" (OPD) | Global | Alliance of OPDs by its own description | https://www.internationaldisabilityalliance.org/content/ida-members and https://www.internationaldisabilityalliance.org/about |
| 2 | IDA regional members: African Disability Forum; Arab Organization of Persons with Disabilities; ASEAN Disability Forum; European Disability Forum; Pacific Disability Forum; RIADIS | Persons with disabilities of a region; RIADIS adds "and their Families"; Pacific Disability Forum: "organisations of and for persons with disabilities" | Cross-disability, geographic | "persons with disabilities" | Regional | As described by IDA; the Pacific forum's "of and for" is flagged | IDA members page (row 1) |
| 3 | World Federation of the Deaf (WFD) | "an international, non-profit, and non-governmental organisation of deaf associations" (IDA's wording); own vision "A World Where Deaf People Everywhere Can Sign Anywhere"; mission "the full realisation of linguistic rights and human rights" | National associations of deaf people | "deaf people"; its youth section speaks of "our linguistic and cultural identity" | Global | "representative organisations of deaf people" (own action plan page) | https://wfdeaf.org/ ; https://wfdeaf.org/who-we-are/ (served at /our-team/); IDA members page |
| 4 | International Federation of Hard of Hearing People (IFHOH) | "all Hard of Hearing Persons"; a member is the All Japan Association of "HOH and late-Deafened People" | Hearing status, as distinct from the signing Deaf community (the page pairs "Deaf and Hard of Hearing People" in a statement title but is a separate federation and a separate IDA member) | "hard of hearing people" | Global | Not stated on the retrieved page | https://www.ifhoh.org/ ; IDA members page |

### 2.3 What the table shows

1. **No retrieved organisation defines its constituency as "people with mobility needs" or "mobility-impaired people".** VERIFIED as an absence in this sample of 27 rows; it is not proof of absence in the world (section 10). Among IDA's eight global constituency members there is none for physical or mobility impairment at all: the eight are blind and partially sighted; deaf; deafblind; hard of hearing; intellectual disability; Down syndrome; spina bifida and hydrocephalus; users and survivors of psychiatry. Physical impairment reaches IDA through the regional cross-disability forums and through one condition-specific body.
2. **Where physically disabled people organise, they use one of four bases.** VERIFIED from rows 11 to 18. Cross-disability (CCD, ENIL). A condition or cause (spinal cord injury; spina bifida; thalidomide; limb loss). A device or form of assistance ("all wheelchair users"; "people who use guide and service dogs"). A political category of physical impairment (UPIAS, 1975: "physically impaired people"; SCI Canada's "and other physical disabilities"). "Physical" has a history as a self-chosen political word. "Mobility" does not appear as one in anything retrieved.
3. **Condition organisations widen toward device and toward cross-disability; they do not narrow toward diagnosis level.** VERIFIED: SCI Canada serves "spinal cord injuries and other physical disabilities"; United Spinal serves "people with SCI/D and all wheelchair users"; ASAN calls itself cross-disability. No retrieved organisation is constituted by paraplegia versus quadriplegia, or by power versus manual chair. INFERRED: those are real and important differences *within* communities; they are not the lines along which the communities draw themselves.
4. **Device-defined constituencies are real, and their edges are contested.** VERIFIED: United Spinal opens membership to all wheelchair users; within it, ambulatory wheelchair users formed their own peer space because of stigma ("why do you use a wheelchair if you can walk?", Rob Henry; "People assume that because I can walk, I don't need my wheelchair or that I'm faking my disability", Annie Segarra; both quoted in row 17's source). A first-person account by Mhairi McKendrick, who has cerebral palsy, describes using a chair for "2 factors: pain and energy levels" ("My life as an ambulatory wheelchair user", Cerebral Palsy Scotland, 28 March 2024, https://cerebralpalsyscotland.org.uk/my-life-as-an-ambulatory-wheelchair-user-mhairi-mckendrick; Cerebral Palsy Scotland itself was not checked for who leads it). A community member quoted by United Spinal says the majority of wheelchair users can stand or walk to some degree; that is her claim, reported, and I did not verify it against data.
5. **Communities choose their own words, and the words differ.** VERIFIED. Identity-first: "autistic people" (ASAN), "disabled people" (ENIL, Sins Invalid), "deaf people" (WFD), "fat people" (NAAFA), "little people" (LPA). Person-first: "people with intellectual disabilities" (Inclusion International), "persons with deafblindness" (WFDB), "people with dementia" (DAI), "people who have limb loss and limb difference" (Amputee Coalition), "persons with disabilities" (IDA, the CRPD). Lydia Brown's article, published by ASAN, gives the reasoning for identity-first use: self-advocates "understand autism as an inherent part of an individual's identity". The registry's display names follow these conventions in most rows; where they do not is noted in section 6.

## 3. Q1 in full: `MOB`

### 3.1 What "mobility" is

"Mobility" names an **activity domain**. VERIFIED in the project's own `identity_icf_map`: every ICF code mapped to `MOB` is a d-code (activities), and the mechanism text is "ambulation, balance, transfer, wheelchair use", four different things. VERIFIED from the Washington Group page: its Short Set deliberately asks about "difficulty functioning in six basic, universal actions", using "the ICF as a framework, focusing on the component of activity limitations", and describes this as "a break from the past and the medicalization of disability that placed disability within the person". The six domains themselves are listed in the questionnaire, which I did not retrieve; that walking is one of them is UNVERIFIED here. VERIFIED from the United Nations text of CRPD Article 20: "personal mobility" is a right to be secured, with access to "mobility aids, devices and assistive technologies", not a class of person.

So `MOB` treats the name of a function and of a right as the name of a people. That is the category error.

### 3.2 What it conflates

| What `MOB` is standing in for | What kind of fact it is | Where the project already has a home for it |
|---|---|---|
| Difficulty walking, balancing, transferring, moving with equipment | Activity (ICF d410 to d470) | `icf_code` lens; `identity_icf_map` (as a map, not as an identity) |
| Paraplegia, tetraplegia, limb absence, spasticity, weakness | Body function and structure; diagnosis and level | `medical_code` lens (demand-populated); ICF b- and s-codes |
| Manual chair, power chair, scooter, walker, prosthesis, crutches | Assistive product; an environmental factor in ICF terms (e120) | `device_class` on the extraction |
| What the building must do: step-free route, turning space, reachable controls, short distances, rest points | Access need | `needs_code` lens (`A-REACH`, `A-EFFORT`, `A-STABLE`, `A-SIZE`) |
| Wheelchair users; people with spinal cord injuries; people with limb loss or limb difference; people with spina bifida; ambulatory wheelchair users | Communities that organise under those names | identity lens: `SCI` and `LMB` exist; the wheelchair-user row was ratified but is not in the registry |

### 3.3 The owner's decomposition, branch by branch

| Owner's example | Kind | Evidence | Is it an identity? |
|---|---|---|---|
| "prosthetics vs wheelchairs vs other mobility aids" | Device | `device_class` already lists chair and walker classes; it has no value for prosthesis, crutches or cane (VERIFIED from the column's CHECK) | The device is not. Behind it, **limb loss and limb difference** is an organised community (Amputee Coalition), and **wheelchair users** are an organised constituency (United Spinal). "Users of other mobility aids": no organisation retrieved. |
| "power wheelchair vs manual wheelchair" | Device and propulsion | See 3.4: turning space varies by drive configuration within power chairs and by frame within manual chairs | No organisation retrieved is constituted this way. Qualitative literature does treat power-chair use as bound up with identity (Rossen et al. 2012; Lindström et al. 2022; abstracts only), so it is identity-*relevant* to individuals without being a community line. |
| "paraplegia vs quadraplegia" | Impairment level | The ledger's own example is a source reporting "17 people with SCI, C4-T12" (2026-09-11 entry) | Not as organised: the retrieved spinal cord injury organisations do not divide by level. I believe "para" and "quad" are in-group terms within that community: UNVERIFIED, not retrieved. For design it matters through trunk control, arm and hand function and thermoregulation, which are ICF b-codes and access needs. |

### 3.4 What the design parameters actually depend on

- **Turning and manoeuvring space depends on the device and its design features.** VERIFIED from the abstract (full text not retrieved) of Koontz et al., "Design Features That Affect the Maneuverability of Wheelchairs and Scooters", *Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation*, 2010: with manual wheelchair, power wheelchair and scooter users, "Ultralight MWCs with rear axles posterior to the shoulder ... required the least amount of space"; "Mid-wheel-drive PWCs required the least space for the 360 degrees-turn in place compared with front-wheel-drive and rear-wheel-drive PWCs"; "PWCs with seat functions required more space"; and "Between 10% and 100% of users would not be able to maneuver in spaces that meet current Accessibility Guidelines". The grouping variable in the analysis is the device's design, not the person's diagnosis or community. (https://consensus.app/papers/details/w:16a1826f-b806-46c7-97fe-171ee59a2273/?utm_source=claude_desktop). The ledger's 2026-09-11 entry quotes this paper's sample line, so the project already holds it; whether it is an admitted source I did not check.
- **Clear floor area depends on occupied device length and width.** VERIFIED from abstracts: D'Souza et al., *Transportation Research Record*, 2010, and Steinfeld et al., *Assistive Technology*, 2010, report current dimensions "inadequate for accommodating many users of wheeled mobility devices, especially those that use power chairs and scooters".
- **Diagnosis does not fix the device.** VERIFIED from the abstract of Martin Ginis et al., *Disability and Rehabilitation*, 2015: among 347 adults with spinal cord injury, those who are ambulatory and those who use manual wheelchairs are distinct subgroups; ambulators are "an often-overlooked subgroup". So `SCI` does not imply a wheelchair, and a wheelchair does not imply `SCI`.
- **Device users sit between categories.** VERIFIED from the abstract of Jang et al., *Disability & Society*, 2019: scooter users experience "liminality", arising partly from their "ambulatory status".
- **Reach depends on seated posture and on trunk and arm function; ramp effort depends on propulsion mode, strength and endurance; handrail and stair use depend on balance and gait.** INFERRED from the access-need definitions in the project's own `access_needs` table and from the ledger's 2026-08-25 entry (ramp gradient opposed between a manual wheelchair user and an ambulant person with fatigue). I retrieved no source on reach or ramp effort in this pass.

**Conclusion for Q1.** For the spatial parameters the corpus holds, the variables that move the number are, in order: the device (class, footprint, drive), the user's function with that device (propulsion, trunk and arm function, endurance), and body size. Community membership moves none of them directly. Community membership matters for a different reason: it says *whose knowledge* the figure came from and *who must be asked* (section 5).

## 4. Q2 in full: do advocates and communities organise this way?

**(a) Cross-disability political identity.** VERIFIED. UPIAS (1975): "it is society which disables physically impaired people. Disability is something imposed on top of our impairments"; "Disabled people are therefore an oppressed group". ENIL: "a user-led network of disabled people", "pan disability". CCD: "of people with all disabilities". ASAN: "Nothing About Us, Without Us!" and "We are One Community". Sins Invalid: "Commitment to Cross-Disability Solidarity ... isolation undermines collective liberation". At this layer the meaningful category is "disabled people", defined by shared exclusion, and impairment type is deliberately not the organising principle.

**(b) Impairment- or condition-specific communities.** VERIFIED for spinal cord injury (rows 15, 16), limb loss and limb difference (18), spina bifida and hydrocephalus (9), autism (19), dementia (20), intellectual disability (7, 21), Down syndrome (8), ME and Long COVID (24), blindness (5), deafblindness (6). These are specific. Not one is as broad as "mobility", "neurological" or "sensory". Cerebral palsy, multiple sclerosis (beyond row 25, which is flagged), muscular dystrophy and polio: organisations exist, I believe, but none was retrieved and confirmed as led by disabled people: UNVERIFIED.

**(c) Device-defined identities.** VERIFIED: "wheelchair user" is a constituency term used by a membership organisation (row 16) and an access description at the same time. It is contested at its edge by ambulatory wheelchair users, who are stigmatised as "faking" (row 17 and the McKendrick account). The project's `AMB`/`WHEEL` cut puts those people on both sides of the line or on neither, as the ledger entry itself says. A second assistance-defined constituency exists in Canada: "People who use Guide and Service Dogs" (row 12). INFERRED: device or assistance use is a legitimate basis for a community row, but because a device is also a physical fact that the extraction records, the two must not be the same cell (rule 5; section 7).

**(d) Administrative and statistical categories.** VERIFIED: the Washington Group's functional domains were built for "comparable data cross-nationally" and to test "whether persons with disability participate to the same extent as persons without disabilities". The page states its own limits: the set will "represent the majority of, but not all, persons with limitation in basic actions", and environmental barriers and participation are "extramural". INFERRED: a functional domain is a sound basis for a design guide's *functional* lens and a poor basis for an *identity* lens, because nobody belongs to a walking-difficulty community. Census "ambulatory difficulty" and benefits categories: not retrieved.

**(e) Critiques of impairment-category taxonomies.**

- *Hierarchy of impairments.* VERIFIED from abstracts: Deal, "Disabled people's attitudes toward other impairment groups: a hierarchy of impairments", *Disability & Society*, 2003: disabled people "do not always wish to be associated with other impairment groups", and research is needed on whether disabled people see themselves "as a homogenous in-group, as a set of separate impairment groups, or viewing impairment as only one facet of identity". Deal's 2006 thesis (City University London) reports a rank ordering among disabled respondents, from most to least accepted: "Deaf, Arthritis, Epilepsy, Cerebral Palsy, HIV/AIDS, Down's Syndrome and Schizophrenia". A classifier that sorts by impairment risks reproducing that ranking in coverage and attention. INFERRED.
- *Deaf people as a linguistic and cultural group.* VERIFIED: WFD's mission is "linguistic rights and human rights"; CRPD Article 30(4) recognises "their specific cultural and linguistic identity, including sign languages and deaf culture". VERIFIED from abstracts: Lane, "Ethnicity, Ethics, and the Deaf-World", *Journal of Deaf Studies and Deaf Education*, 2005, argues against construing the Deaf-World as a disability group ("Deaf people themselves do not believe they have a disability"); Ferri et al., *International and Comparative Law Quarterly*, 2024, find three legal approaches in European Union states (minority, cultural, disability) and note deaf advocacy organisations "eschewing the notion of disability" while WFD itself works inside IDA and the CRPD. The community disagrees with itself here, and the taxonomy should not settle it for them.
- *Neurodiversity.* VERIFIED: ASAN defines the neurodiversity movement as concerning "people with brain-based disabilities (like autism, intellectual disabilities, learning disabilities, or mental health disabilities)", and General Comment No. 7 para 50 writes "neurodiverse persons, including those with autism or dementia". So "neurodivergent" is, by the movement's and the Committee's own usage, a coalition term that spans what the registry codes as `AUT`, `ADHD`, `ID`, `MH` and arguably `DEM`. ASAN also rejects functioning labels ("ASAN doesn't use labels like 'high-functioning' and 'low-functioning'"), which is a warning against severity sub-codes.
- *Users and survivors of psychiatry; mad studies.* VERIFIED: the international organisation names itself by experience of the psychiatric system and by "psychosocial disabilities" (row 10). VERIFIED from abstracts: Davar, *Indian Journal of Gender Studies*, 2008, argues that "A mental illness language has been exhausted of any positive content" and that the rights orientation comes "from disability thinking"; Aubrecht, *Review of Disability Studies*, 2012, examines "the imposition of a language of mental illness". "Mad pride" organisations themselves were not retrieved (MindFreedom returned 404).
- *Access needs and access intimacy.* VERIFIED: Mia Mingus, "Access Intimacy: The Missing Link", *Leaving Evidence*, 5 May 2011 (https://leavingevidence.wordpress.com/2011/05/05/access-intimacy-the-missing-link/): "Access intimacy is that elusive, hard to describe feeling when someone else 'gets' your access needs"; "It doesn't mean that our access looks the same". The unit here is the access need of a person in a relationship, not a category of person. The project's `access_needs` lens is the nearest thing it has to this vocabulary. INFERRED.
- *Epistemic justice.* VERIFIED from abstracts: Scully, *International Journal of Feminist Approaches to Bioethics*, 2018, on "the ascription of a global epistemic incapacity to people affected by impairment"; Chapman and Carel, *Journal of Social Philosophy*, 2022, on hermeneutical injustice, where "a community's shared vocabularies have been structured in a way that unfairly distorts or stifles understanding"; Felder, *Theory and Research in Education*, 2025, on participatory disability research as "a critique and a corrective".
- *Chronic illness, "Spoonie" and fatigue communities; crip theory texts; Protactile and DeafBlind cultural sources; blind-led national federations.* Not retrieved (section 10).

## 5. Q3 in full: what the ethical approaches propose, weighted by the owner's lens

The fourteenth statement puts advocacy groups and disability ethics first. I therefore weight participation and epistemic justice first (who gets to define a category), then the approaches that say what a built-environment guide should classify, then the rest. Sources are those already cited; where an approach's primary texts were not retrieved, that is said.

| Approach | What it holds (source) | What it implies for this taxonomy |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Participation / CRPD Art. 4.3 / Co-1** | States "shall closely consult with and actively involve persons with disabilities ... through their representative organizations" (CRPD Art. 4(3), VERIFIED); organisations are those "led, directed and governed by persons with disabilities" and people "decide for themselves which organizations they want to represent them" (GC7, VERIFIED) | A category of people is legitimate when the people in it chose it. An identity row needs a named community source. A row with none is an administrative label and should not sit in the identity lens. |
| **2. Epistemic justice** | Testimonial and hermeneutical injustice (Scully 2018; Chapman and Carel 2022; abstracts) | Naming a group with a word it does not use is a hermeneutical harm; discounting a Co-1 source because its authors do not fit a code is a testimonial one. The registry should store the community's own name and its source, and the project should expect names to change. |
| **3. Disability justice and intersectionality** | Intersectionality; "Leadership of those most impacted"; "Commitment to cross-disability solidarity"; "Collective access" (Sins Invalid, VERIFIED) | Against single-axis sorting of people: one person holds several identities, and race, gender, age and Indigeneity cut across all of them (GC7 11(e) agrees). Supports many-to-many links, never one code per person or per figure. Pulls *against* impairment-specific codes becoming silos. |
| **4. Social model** | Disability is "imposed on top of our impairments" by social organisation (UPIAS 1975, VERIFIED) | Classify barriers and environmental demands, not bodies. Strongly supports the needs lens as the primary key for determinations. Criticised for neglecting impairment (Furner 2019 summarises and answers the criticisms; Kazou 2017; abstracts), which is why the ICF and medical lenses are still needed. |
| **5. Human-rights model / CRPD** | Persons with disabilities "include those who have long-term physical, mental, intellectual or sensory impairments which in interaction with various barriers may hinder" participation (Art. 1, VERIFIED): an open, interactional description, not a list. Universal design "shall not exclude assistive devices for particular groups of persons with disabilities where this is needed" (Art. 2, VERIFIED). Art. 9 access "on an equal basis with others"; Art. 20 personal mobility; Art. 30(4) linguistic and cultural identity | The Convention uses four very broad impairment words and declines to define a closed set. It names devices and "particular groups" as legitimate objects of design. Supports: needs and barriers first; device as a first-class fact; cultural-linguistic identity respected as such. |
| **6. ICF biopsychosocial model** | Disability at "the interaction between a person's capabilities ... and environmental barriers" (Washington Group page, VERIFIED). It has no place for community or culture, and its personal factors are unclassified. So the ICF lens cannot replace the identity lens; it can replace `MOB`. |
| **7. Universal design and its critiques** | CRPD Art. 2 definition (VERIFIED). Boys, *Journal of Architectural Education*, 2020 (abstract): "Simplistic binary divisions between 'the disabled' and 'everyone else' remain surprisingly normalized" | Universal scale must not erase who a provision was won by and for. | **8. Capabilities approach** | Named in the project's own four-framework rule as the justice framework (ledger, VERIFIED). Primary texts not retrieved: UNVERIFIED beyond that | Asks what each person is actually able to do and be; resists group averages. | **9. Care ethics / relational** | Mingus's access intimacy (VERIFIED); interdependence (Sins Invalid, VERIFIED). A person-only taxonomy misses the pair. |
| **10. Critical disability studies / crip** | Hamraie and Boys as above (abstracts). Crip theory primary texts not retrieved | Categories are made, not found; a classification can produce the thing it claims to describe. Supports holding categories as revisable data with provenance and dates. |

**Where they conflict, plainly.**

1. **Self-definition versus design equivalence.** Approaches 1 and 2 say use the community's category. The project's own rule says group by shared design demand. They diverge: the spinal cord injury community includes ambulatory people and wheelchair users (Martin Ginis et al.); wheelchair users include many conditions. Neither grouping can do the other's job. This is the central finding, and it is why the recommendation gives the two jobs to two different lenses.
2. **Cross-disability solidarity versus specificity.** Disability justice and the social model resist impairment silos; community organisations and the hierarchy-of-impairment evidence show both that specific communities are real and that sorting by impairment can rank people.
3. **Deaf as linguistic minority versus disabled.** Lane's position and WFD's practice differ; the CRPD holds both (Art. 30(4) inside a disability convention).
4. **Identity-first versus person-first.** Not resolvable in general; it differs by community (section 2.3, point 5). The project's rule already defers to each community; keep it.
5. **"Neurodivergent" versus "autistic", and versus "mental health".** The coalition term includes mental health disabilities by ASAN's definition; users and survivors of psychiatry organise separately and under a different word. A taxonomy that makes `NDV`, `AUT` and `MH` three flat peers hides that one is a coalition spanning the other two.
6. **Diagnosis-optional versus diagnosis-required.** The project's membership doctrine is diagnosis-optional, and ASAN includes self-identified autistic people; Dementia Alliance International makes a confirmed diagnosis a condition of membership. Communities differ on this too.
7. **ICF universalism versus community.** The ICF can describe everyone and names no one. Using it alone would satisfy the social model and fail approaches 1 to 3.

## 7. Q5: options, trade-offs, recommendation

| | (1) Keep codes as they are | (2) Identity only where a self-organised community exists; the rest become need / ICF / device descriptors | (3) Hierarchy as data: parent family with children, commonality kept at the parent | (4) Retire identity as a key; needs + ICF key everything; communities are a typed relation for provenance only |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Four lens columns (2026-08-28)** | Unchanged | Unchanged in shape; fewer, better-founded identity values; more rows state `needs_code` / `icf_code` | Unchanged; `parent_code` (already a column, unused) gets used | **Changes a ruled key**: `identity_code` leaves `specifications`. Needs a new owner ruling |
| **Determinations** | Stay keyed on `MOB`; universal-scale rows keep an identity they should not have | Spatial parameters keyed on need / ICF, conditioned on device; identity-keyed only where a community's evidence differs in kind (e.g. sign-language sightlines, Deaf) | A parent-keyed determination is allowed only if the family passes the design-equivalence test; otherwise the parent is navigation only | Cleanest key; loses the ability to state a determination *for* a community where that is what the evidence is |
| **Co-1 attribution** | Carried, if at all, by the same code that keys the figure: who produced and whom it serves are confused | Needs a separate relation, source to community, so that co-production is recorded once and is not inferred from the lens | Same as (2) | Its strongest point: provenance is explicit and separate |
| **Universal / population / person scales** | `ALL` duplicates `universal` | `ALL` leaves the identity lens; universal scale is stated once in `design_scale` | Parent = a population-scale view; children = finer population views | Identity never appears in a key; population scale is expressed by need and ICF |
| **Coverage** | Looks complete; hides who is missing (ambulatory wheelchair users; hard of hearing) | Honest gaps appear: a community with no row is visibly absent; a row with no evidence is visibly thin | Commonality is findable at the parent, as the owner's second statement of 2026-11-12 asks | Coverage counted by need and ICF, which the registry of needs already supports |
| **Rule 5 (device_class versus identity)** | Violated in spirit: "wheelchair users" is in a display name, a ratified code and a device column | Device lives in `device_class` only; a wheelchair-user community row means *the community*, never the device | Device is not a child of an identity | No conflict: device is only ever a device |
| **Flexibility ("no hard-coded behaviours")** | Low: the split is a migration each time | Medium: rows change as communities do | High: depth is data, no code branch per family | High |
| **Risk** | Continues a superseded state; every new row deepens it | Requires a per-row community source, which is real work and, on my evidence, Anglophone-biased until non-English organisations are read | A hierarchy tempts readers to treat the parent as a portrait; the project's irreducibility principle must travel with it | Erases communities from the determination surface, the opposite of what the fourteenth statement asks |

### RECOMMENDATION (for the owner's decision; nothing here is decided)

**Option 2, with option 3's hierarchy held as data, and option 4's separation of provenance from the key.** In the owner's own terms:

1. **Leave the four lens columns as ruled.** No change to the 2026-08-28 key.
2. **Rule what the identity lens may contain: a community that disabled people organised and named themselves.** Each row carries the source it rests on (an organisation of disabled people, a governing document, or a Co-1 publication) and the date read. This is the fourteenth statement's ACTION 2 applied to the registry, and the 2026-07-22 rule ("specific self-identified communities named on their own terms") finally enforced on it. A row without a source is marked as unassessed, not deleted.
3. **Retire `MOB` as an identity.** "Mobility" stays, in the lenses that already hold it: ICF d4 codes and the access needs. Each existing `MOB` row is then judged by what it names, which is what the delegated resolution OD-14 already proposes; this memo adds that for most of the corpus the honest answer is a need and a device, with a community link only where the source names one. The 2026-08-25 ruling is not relitigated here: `WHEEL` is supported by the advocacy evidence (a constituency a membership organisation names). `AMB` is not supported as a self-name; in what I retrieved, "ambulatory" appears as a community word only in "ambulatory wheelchair users", who are exactly the people the binary does not place. That is evidence for the owner, who ruled the split "to start" and has since said `MOB` has more than two levels.
4. **Device in one home.** `device_class` on the extraction is the only place a device is stated. The owner's first two decompositions (aid type; power versus manual) are already that column's vocabulary; it lacks prosthesis, crutches and cane. Whether the list should become a small base registry with a foreign key, so that a prosthesis can be added without a schema change, is a tooling question for a separate change (rule 10).
5. **Impairment level in one home.** Paraplegia versus quadriplegia goes to the medical lens when a source names it (the lens is demand-populated by ruling), and to ICF b-codes for the function it changes. It is not an identity row.
6. **Family as data.** Use `parent_code`, or a typed relation, for families and coalitions: a wheeled-mobility family, the neurodivergent coalition over autistic people, ADHDers and others, body size. A parent is for navigation and for finding commonality "at an abstract level", as the owner's second statement of 2026-11-12 requires. It keys a determination only if it passes the ratified design-equivalence test. Relation types should distinguish "is a coalition that includes" from "is a design-equivalent family of", because `NDV` is the first and `COM` was ratified as the second.
7. **Provenance as its own relation.** Who co-produced a source (the Co-1 warrant) is recorded once, as a link from the source to a community, separate from the lens that says whom a determination serves. The two are different facts; today one code is asked to carry both, and `root_population_note` carries the first in prose.
8. **`ALL` leaves the identity lens** if the owner confirms the hedged 2026-11-06 reading; universal scale is already stated by `design_scale`.
9. **Split the compound cells** (`DEAF`; `LMB`) when their rows are next touched, on the project's own 2026-11-06 schema rule (one value per cell).

**What this does not do.** It does not say which communities to add; that needs a wider and non-English reading of organisations than this pass managed. It does not rank communities. It does not touch `COM` or `BRAIN`, which the owner ratified with eyes open; it only reports that the advocacy lens and the design-equivalence test give different answers for `COM`.

**Confidence and what would change it:** as stated in section 0.

# Population umbrellas: does "mobility" make sense as an identity, and what should the identity lens hold?

**Status:** advisory memo for the owner. Population taxonomy is the owner's doctrine: this memo RECOMMENDS and decides nothing. It changes no file, row, ruling or task.
**Written:** 2026-11-12, by a Fable-class researcher-analyst, in answer to the owner's two questions of that day and under the owner's statements "thirteenth" (MOB decomposes) and "fourteenth" ("use advocacy groups and disability ethics as a lens for grouping/sorting/taxonomy").
**Drift warning:** every statement about the database was read from `data/guidebook.db` on 2026-11-12 (read-only). No count is quoted as a fact to trust; each carries the command that regenerates it (section 9). Every web source was retrieved on 2026-11-12; nothing was written to the retrieval log or the database, so nothing here is an admitted source.

**Claim marks.** VERIFIED = I retrieved the page or record and read the passage. INFERRED = my reasoning, basis stated. UNVERIFIED = I believe it but did not retrieve it; do not rely on it.

**The unratified assumption this memo works under** (ledger, fourteenth statement): "advocacy groups" means disabled people's own organisations, the CRPD's "representative organizations", not charities or service bodies speaking for them. The CRPD Committee draws that line itself (General Comment No. 7, paras 11 and 13, section 2.1). Every organisation below is flagged where the retrieved page did not show it to be led by disabled people.

---

## 0. Verdict

**Q1. Does "mobility" make sense as an identity population? No.** In the sources retrieved, disabled people do not organise as "people with mobility needs". They organise across disability (Council of Canadians with Disabilities, ENIL), by condition or impairment (spinal cord injury, spina bifida and hydrocephalus, limb loss and limb difference), and by device ("all wheelchair users", United Spinal Association). "Mobility" is the name of a functional domain (ICF chapter d4, the Washington Group's walking question, CRPD Article 20 on personal mobility as a right). `MOB` conflates four different kinds of fact: a function, a set of impairments, the use of an assistive device, and a number of separate communities. The owner's decomposition is correct, but its branches are not all identities: aid type and power-versus-manual are **device** facts; paraplegia-versus-quadriplegia is an **impairment-level** fact; only some branches (limb loss and limb difference, spinal cord injury, wheelchair users) correspond to communities that organise under that name. The design parameters the project has actually researched depend on the device and its user's function, not on a community.

**Q2. Do contemporary advocates think like this? Not in this form.** They hold several layers at once: a cross-disability political identity ("disabled people", "nothing about us without us"); specific communities named on their own terms, some of which reject the impairment frame altogether (Deaf people as a linguistic and cultural group; users and survivors of psychiatry rather than "people with mental health conditions"); device-defined constituencies whose edges are contested (ambulatory wheelchair users); and, separately, functional categories that statisticians use and that advocates treat as tools, not identities. Broad impairment umbrellas ("mobility", "neurological", "mental health") are the administrative layer, not the self-defined one.

**Q3. What do modern ethical approaches propose?** They converge on three points and disagree on a fourth. (1) Classify the **environment's demand and the barrier**, not the person (social model, CRPD, ICF environmental factors, universal design). (2) Where people are named, **they name themselves**, through their own organisations (CRPD Art. 4.3 and General Comment No. 7, epistemic justice, disability justice's "leadership of those most impacted"). (3) Keep the **individual** in view: categories are retrieval aids, never portraits (capabilities approach, care ethics, crip critique, the project's own irreducibility principle). They disagree on (4) whether impairment-specific categories should exist at all: disability justice and the social model press toward cross-disability solidarity and warn about hierarchies of impairment; community self-definition and the capabilities approach press toward specificity. The reconciliation the evidence supports is to keep the two jobs apart: communities for **voice and provenance**, access needs / ICF / device for **design parameters**.

**RECOMMENDATION (the owner decides).** Keep the four lens columns exactly as ruled on 2026-08-28. Change what the **identity** lens is allowed to contain: only communities that disabled people have organised and named themselves, each row carrying the organisation or ethical source it rests on as provenance (the fourteenth statement's own ACTION 2). Retire `MOB` as an identity; hold "mobility" where it already lives, as ICF d4 codes and access needs. Hold device in `device_class` and nowhere else. Hold family resemblance (the "mobility family", the "neurodivergent" coalition) as a parent relation in data, used for navigation and for finding commonality, never as the key of a determination unless the family passes the ratified design-equivalence test. Record who co-produced a source as a typed relation to a community, separately from whom a determination serves. This is option 2 with option 3's hierarchy held as data, and option 4's separation of provenance from the key (section 7).

**Confidence.** High (about 85%) that `MOB` is not an identity and that device and impairment level are not identities. Moderate (about 70%) that restricting the identity lens to self-organised communities is the right rule. Low to moderate (about 50%) on the particular list of communities, because my sample of organisations is international-umbrella and Anglophone (Canada, United States, United Kingdom, Europe), no non-English national organisation was retrieved, and several key organisations could not be reached (section 10).

**What would change it.** (a) Evidence that organisations *of* physically disabled people, as such, are a common form outside English (the United Kingdom's Union of the Physically Impaired Against Segregation, 1975, is one; I did not retrieve any current national federation of this kind, and I think it likely that several exist: UNVERIFIED). That would support a "physical disability" community row, though still not "mobility". (b) Co-1 evidence that a design parameter varies by community membership after device and function are held fixed. (c) The owner ruling that the identity lens is meant as a reader's entry point rather than as a statement about communities, in which case administrative umbrellas are tolerable as entry aliases, provided they key nothing.

---

## 1. What the project's own rulings and rows say (read first, so the rest is not relitigated)

All VERIFIED by reading `references/project-standards.md` (locate each with the grep in section 9) and the database.

1. **Work from axes, no armchair umbrellas** (2026-07-22). The profile layer "is populated only with specific self-identified communities named on their own terms (co-produced; 'nothing about us without us')". "Physically disabled / wheelchair users" is named there as one of three self-caught erasures.
2. **Design-equivalence exception** (2026-07-23). An umbrella is permitted only if (a) high comorbidity or near-identical design profile, (b) the union of member signatures is preserved, (c) no opposed demand between members. `COM` and `BRAIN` were ratified under it.
3. **`MOB` is split** into ambulatory (`AMB`) and wheelchair user (`WHEEL`), "to start" (2026-08-25, marked not to be relitigated). The entry itself says `MOB` fails clause (c) and that part-time wheelchair users and balance are covered by neither new code.
4. **"Population" is retired; four lenses** identity / icf / needs / medical; four typed lens columns with real foreign keys; CHECK relaxed to at least one (2026-08-28, D-0182).
5. **The medical lens grows on demand**, and the ledger already observed that the wheeled-mobility literature "studies wheelchairs, scooters and walking aids, not diagnoses" (2026-09-11).
6. **`ALL` is a scope marker, not a population** (2026-11-06, hedged by the owner).
7. **Thirteenth and fourteenth statements** (2026-11-12): `MOB` is a family with more than two levels; advocacy groups and disability ethics are the lens. The thirteenth entry's own ACTION 3 already says a division describing a device or a participant's level is kept in one home (rule 5) and that whether it is an identity or a descriptor is the owner's to decide.

**The registry does not match the rulings.** VERIFIED:

- `base_taxonomy_identity` still carries `MOB` as `active`, and carries no `AMB` or `WHEEL` row, although the split was ratified on 2026-08-25. `parent_code` is empty on every row.
- `MOB` carries the large majority of `source_value_extractions` rows; the other identity codes in use there are `ALL`, `SCI`, `BLIND` and `MS`, each with a handful.
- Almost every extraction states the identity lens only; the ICF and needs lenses are used on a handful of rows and the medical lens on none. The project's rule is to work from the ICF and access-need frame; the rows work from the umbrella.
- `device_class` is filled on a minority of the `MOB` rows; where it is filled the values in use are `manual_self_propelled`, `mixed` and `not_device_scoped`. The column's CHECK also allows `manual_attendant`, `power_chair`, `scooter`, `bariatric_manual`, `bariatric_power` and `walker_rollator`, none of which is in use. So the registry of devices exists, as a CHECK list, and already holds the first two of the owner's three decompositions (aid type; power versus manual).
- What the `MOB` rows actually name, from `root_population_note` where filled: manual self-propelled wheelchair users; "eleven wheelchair users; chair types not stated"; thirteen wheelchair users of whom at least one used a motorised chair; a first-person judgment by a manual wheelchair user about experienced self-propelling users; an aggregate of eight subject groups that "is not a wheelchair-only recommendation"; and organisations whose constituency is wider than wheelchair users (people with any disability or chronic illness) or different (people with intellectual disability). None names "people with mobility needs". The code is being used to mean "this is about getting about, mostly on wheels".
- Every `specifications` row is keyed on `MOB`, all are retired, and most state `design_scale = 'universal'`. A determination at universal scale keyed on an identity states two things that cannot both be meant: universal is the scale that names no group.
- `identity_icf_map` grades `MOB` to nine ICF d-codes (d410 to d530) as `high_predictive`. That is the highest confidence grade, given to a category the ledger says fails the umbrella test because its members' demands are opposed. Walking (d450), using equipment to move (d465), washing (d510) and toileting (d530) cannot all be predicted with high confidence from membership of a set that includes a prosthesis user, a power-chair user with tetraplegia and a person with a balance disorder. INFERRED from the map and the ledger entry.

## 2. The lens: how disabled people's own organisations define their constituencies

### 2.1 What counts as an organisation of disabled people

VERIFIED from the United Nations document CRPD/C/GC/7, *General comment No. 7 (2018) on the participation of persons with disabilities, including children with disabilities, through their representative organizations, in the implementation and monitoring of the Convention*, Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, distributed 9 November 2018 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3899396/files/CRPD_C_GC_7-EN.pdf):

- Para 11: organisations of persons with disabilities "can only be those that are led, directed and governed by persons with disabilities. A clear majority of their membership should be recruited among persons with disabilities themselves."
- Para 11(d): "They may represent one or more constituencies based on actual or perceived impairment or can be open to membership of all persons with disabilities". Para 11(e): they "can include constituencies based on transversal identities (for example, children, women or indigenous people with disabilities) and comprise members with various impairments".
- Para 12 names the types: umbrella organisations (which "only speak on behalf of their member organizations" and "cannot represent individual persons with disabilities"); cross-disability organisations; self-advocacy organisations, "especially persons with intellectual disabilities"; organisations including family members, for people with intellectual disabilities, dementia and children, whose role "should be to assist and empower"; organisations of women and girls; organisations of children and young persons. Para 12(a) adds: "persons with disabilities should be able to decide for themselves which organizations they want to represent them."
- Para 13: they "should be distinguished from organizations 'for' persons with disabilities, which provide services and/or advocate on behalf of persons with disabilities, which, in practice, may result in a conflict of interests".
- Para 50 gives the Committee's own list of who must be reached. It is not a taxonomy and mixes kinds freely: women, older persons, children, "those requiring high levels of support", victims of landmines, migrants, "persons with actual or perceived psychosocial impairments, persons with intellectual disabilities, neurodiverse persons, including those with autism or dementia, persons with albinism, permanent physical impairments, chronic pain, leprosy and visual impairments and persons who are deaf, deafblind or otherwise hearing-impaired".

Three things follow for a taxonomy. INFERRED from the paragraphs above. (i) The Committee accepts **three bases of constituency at once**: impairment ("actual or perceived"), open cross-disability membership, and transversal identity. It does not rank them. (ii) Constituency is **self-chosen**: the test is who leads and whom people choose to represent them, not which box a classifier puts them in. (iii) An umbrella speaks only for its members on agreed matters and cannot represent individuals. That is the Committee's version of this project's own anti-umbrella rule.

Among IDA's eight global constituency members there is none for physical or mobility impairment at all: the eight are blind and partially sighted; deaf; deafblind; hard of hearing; intellectual disability; Down syndrome; spina bifida and hydrocephalus; users and survivors of psychiatry. Physical impairment reaches IDA through the regional cross-disability forums and through one condition-specific body.
2. **Where physically disabled people organise, they use one of four bases.** VERIFIED from rows 11 to 18. Cross-disability (CCD, ENIL). A condition or cause (spinal cord injury; spina bifida; thalidomide; limb loss). A device or form of assistance ("all wheelchair users"; "people who use guide and service dogs"). A political category of physical impairment (UPIAS, 1975: "physically impaired people"; SCI Canada's "and other physical disabilities"). "Physical" has a history as a self-chosen political word. "Mobility" does not appear as one in anything retrieved.
3. **Condition organisations widen toward device and toward cross-disability; they do not narrow toward diagnosis level.** VERIFIED: SCI Canada serves "spinal cord injuries and other physical disabilities"; United Spinal serves "people with SCI/D and all wheelchair users"; ASAN calls itself cross-disability. No retrieved organisation is constituted by paraplegia versus quadriplegia, or by power versus manual chair. INFERRED: those are real and important differences *within* communities; they are not the lines along which the communities draw themselves.
4. **Device-defined constituencies are real, and their edges are contested.** VERIFIED: United Spinal opens membership to all wheelchair users; within it, ambulatory wheelchair users formed their own peer space because of stigma ("why do you use a wheelchair if you can walk?", Rob Henry; "People assume that because I can walk, I don't need my wheelchair or that I'm faking my disability", Annie Segarra; both quoted in row 17's source). A first-person account by Mhairi McKendrick, who has cerebral palsy, describes using a chair for "2 factors: pain and energy levels" ("My life as an ambulatory wheelchair user", Cerebral Palsy Scotland, 28 March 2024, https://cerebralpalsyscotland.org.uk/my-life-as-an-ambulatory-wheelchair-user-mhairi-mckendrick; Cerebral Palsy Scotland itself was not checked for who leads it). A community member quoted by United Spinal says the majority of wheelchair users can stand or walk to some degree; that is her claim, reported, and I did not verify it against data.
5. **Communities choose their own words, and the words differ.** VERIFIED. Identity-first: "autistic people" (ASAN), "disabled people" (ENIL, Sins Invalid), "deaf people" (WFD), "fat people" (NAAFA), "little people" (LPA). Person-first: "people with intellectual disabilities" (Inclusion International), "persons with deafblindness" (WFDB), "people with dementia" (DAI), "people who have limb loss and limb difference" (Amputee Coalition), "persons with disabilities" (IDA, the CRPD). Lydia Brown's article, published by ASAN, gives the reasoning for identity-first use: self-advocates "understand autism as an inherent part of an individual's identity". The registry's display names follow these conventions in most rows; where they do not is noted in section 6.
